title: Start with the question
text: We have rainfall readings: 5, 22, 20 and 45 millimetres. For this programming exercise, collect the readings strictly greater than 20. Twenty is an example threshold, not a weather classification or a school-closure rule.

title: Remember progress
text: Create an empty list named heavy before the loop. This list remembers the qualifying readings we have found so far. Creating it inside the loop would throw away previous progress.

title: Inspect one reading at a time
text: A for loop gives mm the next reading on each iteration. Ask whether mm is greater than 20. Five fails. Twenty-two passes. Exactly twenty fails. Forty-five passes.

title: Change the list
text: When the comparison is true, append mm to heavy. Append changes the same list object. After twenty-two, heavy contains twenty-two. After forty-five it contains twenty-two and forty-five.

title: Return the result
text: Return heavy after the loop finishes, so the caller receives the completed list. Printing displays text; returning sends a value to the caller. Returning inside the loop ends the function before all readings have been inspected.

title: Change what you remember
text: For a counting task, remember a number instead of a list. Start a count at zero before the loop, increase it by one when a reading qualifies, and return the count after the loop. The comparison stays the same; the accumulated state changes.

title: Apply the idea elsewhere
text: Python strings can also be placed in a list. The expression len(name) returns the number of characters in a name. After reviewing this prerequisite, use the same inspect, compare and remember pattern to collect names longer than six characters.
